superficial: A fired-clay tablet, one of the first the Institute learned to read. The Teacher always keeps it at hand for new students.
"Irrigation shifts of the waxing quarter: the Aren, at dawn. The Tolu, mid-morning. The Imre, at sunset."
Beside every shift, the same small mark, repeated.
profunda: Now you recognize the small mark: it is the mark of the Gates.
"At dawn, the irrigation; and then, the Gate." They crossed to go to work, to come back to eat, to visit someone.
Each irrigation, a trip. Each trip, a little more debt.

superficial: Two carved stones, from two different arrivals. Both have a smooth, curved edge, as if someone had scooped a piece out of a sphere with a spoon.
The label reads: "Cut of unknown origin. No known tool leaves it like this."
profunda: They are not broken ruins. They are bites: the space over there, torn out in perfect spheres by the small wormholes that open when the debt leaks.
Every curved edge is the footprint of a mouth that opened for an instant.

superficial: A pale slab with the lower half of a ring of lines, like those of a clock, cut off at the top in a curve.
Nobody at the Institute knows what it means. The Teacher says that what matters is what is missing.
profunda: The other half is still there, on the wall of a bite at the Scar. They fit line to line.
This stone did not travel: it was torn from the world where the black hole is born.

superficial: Institute report, unfinished: the translation of a technical plaque of the Absent.
"Every step leaves a debt that..." The rest is broken.
In the margin, in the Director's hand: "Energy cost. Compensated by the test room generator."
profunda: It was not energy. The debt is one of time: every step drifts the clocks of the two mouths a little further apart.
The margin still says "compensated." Nobody at home yet knows with what.

superficial: On the workshop table, a brass ring the size of a hand, held in clamps and full of wires. Beside it, a stack of sheets: "Minor test 3: the ring opened for eleven seconds. No incidents."
On the blackboard, circled three times: "Great test, in forty days."
profunda: They are rebuilding a Gate from plans that arrived in pieces, and they are missing exactly the piece that keeps it stable.
Forty days. That is the time you have to get back.

superficial: The Director is waiting for you at the Engine, at the foot of the Great Gate, looking at the Moon above the Institute's hill.
"Yesterday the largest fragment of all appeared up there, stuck in the ground. I want you to see it before anyone else: it will be your first official flight."
"The Albatross II is ready in the hangar. Go, look, and come back and tell me."
profunda: She speaks of the great test the way others speak of a child. She has been preparing it for years: it is the one that will greet those who left all this behind.
If anyone has to hear the truth, it is her. And she is the one who will least want to hear it.

superficial: "Have you read the irrigation tablet yet? Always start there: the everyday is what is best understood."
"We have read their language for years and still do not know how they laughed. That is not on any stone."
"Go and see the Director before she runs out of patience. And come back and tell me everything, all right?"
"The small ring now holds open eleven seconds in a row. Eleven!"
"The Director says that in the great test we will greet whoever made all this. I only ask that the mount does not melt."
"The Albatross II is ready: tanks full and the reliquary empty, waiting for your fragment."
"Climb in with F. In there the dashboard tells you everything: aim at the Moon with T and, if everything spins, Z steadies it."
"And do not scratch her. She is the only one we have."
"They say another of those stones fell on the Moon yesterday. Bigger than a house."
"My grandfather found one in the vegetable garden, one of the first. He used it to prop the door. Now it is in a display case."
"I mended the elbow of your suit last night. Make sure it does not tear again on the Moon."
"When you come back, tell me what color the light is up there. I want to dye something that color."
"Will you bring me a stone from the Moon? A small one! I promise not to show it to anyone."
"The sea is stiller than ever. My grandmother used to say that when the sea goes quiet, something big is listening."
"Today everyone has come out to the square to see you take off. Act natural, or they will get nervous."
A notebook with worn covers, open beside the spyglass. The handwriting is small and cramped.
"Today they went up to look at the Moon again, not moving, filaments glowing, thinking nobody notices."
"Of all the new students, they were the one who asked me who does the watering on the other side. I still do not know what to answer."
"When they come back, I will tell them: that I knew this day would come."

hogar.plano_albatros.titulo: The plan of the first Albatross
superficial: A blue plan pinned to the wall: a round ship, smaller than the one in the hangar. At the top it says "Albatross".
Underneath, in pencil: "Lost in the altitude test, to the west, beyond the sea. Nobody was hurt. Nobody went to look for it."
And in another hand, newer: "That is why the current one is called the second."
Under the tarp, charcoal drawings: the Moon, some stars, a ship with a lantern. There are more drawings than room.
On a board, in a child's hand: "Club of those who look up. Only rule: do not tell the grown-ups."
One of the names on the list is circled twice. It is yours.
A stone Ool with an open book; water falls from its pages. The plaque is worn from being touched so often.
"To Ilen, who read the first word of those who are not here. The word was: water."
The city children say that if you ask it something in a low voice, its stone filaments light up.
The irrigation shifts of this moon, hand-painted: "The village, at dawn. The city, mid-morning. The Institute, at sunset."
Below, someone has added: "As on the clay tablet. If it went well for them, it will go well for us."
Nobody has written what they did after watering.
A greenish brass bell, half buried in the sand of the seabed. It must have been the old lighthouse's.
Around the rim, some letters: "Ring when the sea goes quiet."
Now the sea is quiet. And the bell, down here, cannot ring.
A label tied with wire to a twisted mount, as if melted and cooled again.
"Minor test 1: the ring opened for two seconds and the mount melted. Do not throw away. We learn from what breaks, too. —T."
Around it, half-built rings, generator drums and gears. All with their label, all in the same hand.
The pages are swollen with damp, but the ink holds.
"Altitude test. On the way up, the mast lantern went out and the wind carried me west. I came down at night on an island where the plants give light."
"I am staying here until they come. There is water, and the night is lovely."
The last page: "They have come. I am leaving. I leave the notebook in case someone else gets lost: let them know that this is home too."
A ring of mossy stones around a shallow pit with a smooth, curved edge.
"Here appeared the first stone of those who are not here, two hundred winters ago. Nobody saw it fall: one morning, it was there."
"They took it to the Institute. We kept the pit."
Slate sheets with chalk dots: stars, noted night after night for years.
On the last one: "Night of the Moon's great stone. The sky, still; not a single star moved. I note it anyway: let it be known that I waited."
"A visitor. It has been years. Did the Director send you? No, I see she did not: curiosity brought you."
"Forty years watching the sky and I have never seen one of those stones fall. They do not fall. They appear, like someone leaving something at another's door."
"Come back and tell me, if you ever find out."
A lone bench in the middle of the lights. On the backrest there is a sentence carved with a knife point.
"You cannot see the Moon from here. That is why we came."
